claims.text: Controlled chemical dealloying of a multicomponent precursor containing noble and sacrificial elements can produce HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
The resulting HEA nanoframeworks can have enhanced catalytic properties.
An acidic or basic solution can preferentially dissolve the less noble sacrificial elements from the precursor.
Controlling solution concentration, temperature, and duration can selectively remove sacrificial components without compromising the residual framework.
Removal of sacrificial elements produces a bicontinuous nanoporous architecture.
The bicontinuous nanoporous architecture increases surface area and the availability of catalytically active sites.
Selective dissolution creates a three-dimensional porous structure in the residual HEA material.
Increased surface area and the resulting elemental arrangement promote synergistic interactions.
These synergistic interactions boost catalytic activity.
Dealloyed HEA nanoframeworks will exhibit better catalytic performance than HEAs produced without dealloying.
Dealloyed HEA nanoframeworks will exhibit better stability than HEAs produced without dealloying.
Controlled nanoporosity and enhanced active surface area cause the predicted improvements in catalytic performance and stability.
HEA catalysts produced without dealloying typically have less controlled surface structures.
HEA catalysts produced without dealloying typically have lower catalytic activity.
Successful nanoframework formation requires an adequate proportion of sacrificial elements.
Dealloying parameters must be tuned to avoid complete dissolution or structural collapse.
